## Inference of molecular gas masses

In light of the detection of multiple emission lines, along with the dust continuum, we are able to derive the molecular gas mass via three different independent approaches. The inferred molecular gas masses are summarized in Table [3](#tab:mmol_mass). The three approaches are based on several different assumptions and the results are in tension (see Section [3.3.4](#sec:mol_mass_sys_error)).

### The Atomic Carbon approach

The emission lines of atomic carbon,  and , are tracers of molecular gas (cite: Papadopoulos2004a; Papadopoulos2004b) in galaxies (cite: Valentino2020). The derivation of molecular gas mass from atomic carbon requires first the estimation of atomic carbon mass, for which the excitation temperature ($\Tex$) must be used to properly constrain the population at the ground state. The detection of both atomic carbon fine-structure transition lines,  and , allows the determination of $\Tex$ under the assumption of local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE). As derived in the Appendix of (cite: Schneider2003), by assuming that both of the two  lines are optically thin, $\Tex$ can be obtained using $$\begin{equation}
    \Tex\,[\text{K}]=\frac{38.8}{\text{ln}(2.11/R)} \label{eqt:T_ex}
\end{equation}$$ where $R$ is the ratio between  and  line luminosities $L^{'}$ in units of K$\cdot$km s$^{-1}$$\cdot$pc$^2$. We used equation (3) in (cite: Solomon1992) to convert the observed line fluxes into line luminosities and derived $R\,=\,0.84\,\pm\,0.20$ and $\Tex=44\,\pm\,16$ K, where the errors indicate the uncertainty from line flux measurements.

Following (cite: Weiss2003), we obtained the atomic carbon mass  $=\,(4.1\,\pm\,0.8)\times10^{7}\,\text{M\ensuremath{_\odot}}$ from the line luminosity of  and $\Tex$ using $$\begin{equation}
    \text{\mCI}\,[\text{M\ensuremath{_\odot}}]=4.566\times10^{-4}Q(\Tex)\frac{1}{5}e^{62.5/\Tex}L^{'}_{\text{\CItwoone}}
\end{equation}$$ where $Q(\Tex)\,=\,1+3e^{-23.6/\Tex}+5e^{-62.5/\Tex}$ is the partition function of atomic carbon.[^5] To get the molecular gas mass , we adapted the atomic carbon abundance $\,=\,3\times10^{-5}$ as derived by (cite: Weiss2003) for M82, and included the correction factor 1.36 for the Helium and heavier elements. This gives $\,=\,(3.1\pm0.6)\times10^{11}\text{M\ensuremath{_\odot}}$. This value is nearly an order of magnitude higher than that published in (cite: Man2019), which is based on shallower ALMA observations of the  emission line. In Appendix [6](#sec:CI_comparison), we provide a detailed description of the factors contributing to this discrepancy.

Some recent studies (cite: Papadopoulos2022; Dunne2022) have raised the concern that the LTE assumption in this  approach is inadequate and that the  alone is not a good tracer for the molecular gas mass due to the large variation in $Q_{21}$. Those studies suggest that using  and a conversion factor $Q_{10}=0.48\,\pm\,0.08$ instead provides a more robust estimation of . As a check of the validity of our approach, we compute the corresponding $Q_{10}$ factor from our  lines and the LTE assumption. Our value, $Q_{10}=0.44\,\pm\,0.02$, is 8 percent lower than (cite: Papadopoulos2022)’s suggested value. Therefore, our estimated value of  is unlikely to be significantly impacted by our LTE assumption. Nonetheless, the  approach does suffer from systematic errors, as discussed in Section [3.3.4](#sec:mol_mass_sys_error).

### The CO approach

The rotational lines of CO have been used extensively to probe the condition of the ISM and the mass of molecular gas (cite: Bolatto2013). This estimation of mass relies on the CO-to-H$_{2}$ factor, $\alphaCO\equiv$ $/\LineLum{\COonezero}$, to convert the line luminosity of  to molecular gas mass[^6]. Since we do not have observations of the  line, an extra step must be taken to convert $\LineLum{\COfourthree}$ to $\LineLum{\COonezero}.$[^7] The exact value for this conversion varies across galaxy types and depends on the ISM conditions. Here we adopt the average value in the literature derived for sub-millimeter galaxies (SMGs) similar to , i.e. $r_{41}\equiv\LineLum{\COfourthree}/\LineLum{\COonezero}=0.46$ (cite: Carilli2013). This gives $\LineLum{\COonezero}=(9.1\pm1.1)\times10^{10}$ K$\cdot$km s$^{-1}$$\cdot$pc$^2$. For $\alphaCO$, we adopted the value commonly used for starburst galaxies, 0.8 M$_\odot$/(K$\cdot$km s$^{-1}$$\cdot$pc$^2$) (cite: Bolatto2013). The final derived  is $(7.3\ \pm\ 0.9)\times10^{10}$M$_\odot$, which is a factor of $\approx$4 smaller than the mass obtained from the  lines.

### The dust emission approach

The dust continuum in the far-infrared/sub-millimeter range can provide an alternative way of estimating the molecular gas mass (cite: Scoville2016). The frequency range covered by ALMA Band 4 and Band 6 corresponds to the Rayleigh-Jeans tail of the modified black-body emission for typical ISM dust temperatures (a few tens of K), which is usually optically thin. The optically thin property provides a linear scaling relation of molecular gas mass  and dust emission luminosity $L_{\text{dust}}$ at a fixed frequency, assuming a fixed dust-to-gas abundance ratio. (cite: Scoville2016) used a sample of 72 galaxies, including local star-forming galaxies, low-z ultraluminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs), and SMGs, to calibrate the dust-to-gas ratio $L_{\text{dust,850\um}}/\text{\mmol}=\alphadust$ and found a remarkably similar value across different galaxy types. Here we use $\alphadust=6.7\cdot10^{19}$ erg s$^{-1}$ Hz$^{-1}$ M$_\odot$$^{-1}$ and equation (16) in (cite: Scoville2016) to derive the molecular gas mass: $$\begin{align}
M_{\mathrm{mol}}=& 1.78\,S_{\nu_{\text{obs}}}\,[\text{mJy}]\ (1+z)^{-4.8} \nonumber\\
              & \times\left(\frac{\nu_{850\text{\um}}}{\nu_{\text{obs}}}\right)^{3.8}\ (D_{L}\,[\text{Gpc}])^{2} \nonumber\\
              & \times\left(\frac{6.7\times10^{19}\,\text{erg\,s$^{-1}$\,Hz$^{-1}$\,M\ensuremath{_\odot}$^{-1}$}}{\alphadust}\right)\ \frac{\Gamma_{0}}{\Gamma_{\text{RJ}}}\ 10^{10}\text{M\ensuremath{_\odot}}
\end{align}$$ where $\Gamma_{0}=0.71$ and $\Gamma_{\text{RJ}}$ is the ratio of blackbody radiation and Rayleigh-Jeans tail assuming a mass-weighted dust temperature of $\Td=25$ K. As mentioned in Sec. [3.1](#sec:cont_fit), the Band 4 dust continuum emission is potentially contaminated by the synchrotron component. We thus derived the molecular gas mass from the Band 6 dust continuum to be  = (2.2 $\pm$ 0.2)$\times10^{11}$M$_\odot$.

### Uncertainties of the inferred molecular gas mass

The molecular gas mass inferred using three different tracers are all subject to systematic uncertainties. For the atomic carbon approach, the excitation of atomic carbon may not be well-constrained from the line ratio alone due to the potential sub-thermal excitation in the diffuse gas (cite: Papadopoulos2022). The abundance of atomic carbon, , which depends on the metallicity, further affects the conversion from  to . For the CO approach, systematic uncertainties are inherent in the assumed excitation condition, $r_{41}$ (cite: Narayanan2014), and the $\alphaCO$ factor, the latter having a metallicity dependence as does atomic carbon (cite: Bolatto2013). Moreover, the use of the line ratio to infer the gas temperature in the atomic carbon approach, and the reliance on an assumed $r_{41}$ in the CO approach, both require the implicit assumption that the measured line fluxes are representative of the entire galaxy and that the line ratios are computed as globally averaged quantities. In reality, different line fluxes may be the most prominent in different spatial regions with different physical conditions. The computation of line ratios across different regions may thus introduce further systematic errors. For the dust emission approach, the systematic error arises from the assumed dust temperature, emissivity, and spectral index, $\alpha = 1.8$, used to infer the strength of dust emission at $850\,$. Those effects manifest themselves collectively in the error of conversion factor $\alphadust$, which according to the calibration provided by (cite: Scoville2016) is 26 percent.

Amongst the three different estimates of  (Table [3](#tab:mmol_mass)), the one inferred from CO is the most discrepant from that of  and dust, being lower by a factor of $\approx4$ and $3$, respectively. This discrepancy can be mitigated by having a higher $\alphaCO$ value or lower $r_{41}$ in the $L_{\rm CO(4-3)}$ to  conversion. (cite: Dunne2022) conducted a cross-calibration of the three  tracers (i.e CO (1-0), , and dust continuum) using a sample of 407 metal-rich galaxies including SMGs like . Contrary to previous studies, they report that a universal Milky-Way like $\alphaCO$ value of 4.0 is adequate and there is no evidence for a bimodal $\alphaCO$ as claimed in many previous studies. Indeed, in  adopting an $\alphaCO$=4.0 will increase the  by a factor of 5, bringing the inferred  to be in agreement with  and dust estimates. On the other hand, adopting a Milky Way value $r_{41}=0.17$ (cite: Carilli2013) instead of the SMG-value will bring the inferred  estimate up by a factor of $\approx2.7$ closer to the other two values. Some high-redshift dusty star-forming galaxies are found to have higher observed  fluxes that than accounted for in the large velocity gradient modeling that uses high-$J$ CO lines alone, which could indicate the presence of a reservoir of diffuse, low-excitation gas (cite: Canameras2018). Therefore, a potential cold gas component with little high-$J$ CO excitation may also explain the  discrepancies in our  and CO approaches.

An alternative explanation for the molecular gas mass discrepancy is that the values inferred using  and dust are both over-estimated relative to that of CO. Indeed, using the same ALMA observations of  presented in this work, Lin et al. (accepted in A&A) reported a dynamical mass of $\sim10^{11}$ M$_\odot$ within the central $3.5$ kpc in  (see also Sec. [4](#sec:discussion)). The total baryonic mass budget, including stellar and gas masses, exceeds the dynamical mass. The lower molecular mass derived using CO may therefore be more appropriate. Adopting a Milky Way value of $=1.6\times10^{-5}$ as reported in (cite: Dunne2022) would bring the  inferred from  up by a factor of $\approx1.9$, which increases the tension with the dust-inferred . Alleviating the tension would require hotter dust than the currently assumed $\Td=25$ K and hence higher $\Gamma_{\rm RJ}$ and/or lower $\alphadust$. To properly constrain the integrated dust properties, high-resolution continuum observations across frequencies are needed to improve the SED fitting done in (cite: Falkendal2019).

## Line ratios

The ratio between the  and CO lines can be used to infer the molecular gas excitation conditions. In particular, the  to  luminosity ratio probes the gas excitation temperature.

We compare these spatially-integrated line ratios of  with those of the compilation of high-redshift galaxies presented in (cite: Valentino2020), which include main-sequence, starburst, active galactic nucleus/quasar, and SMGs (see their Sec. 2 for a detailed description of their sample selection). The comparison of the line ratios are shown in Fig. [4](#fig:emission_line_compare). Due to the heterogeneity in the galaxy types and observations in their compilation, a galaxy is only plotted if it has a detection in both quantities of the axes in each panel. Overall,  has relatively high emission line luminosities, as expected for its high SFR, similar to the SMG sample. The only exception is that its $\LineLum{\COsevensix}$ and $\LineLum{\COfourthree}$ are generally at the faint end of the SMG sample, similar to the three QSOs shown in the leftmost panel of Fig. [4](#fig:emission_line_compare). The / ratio of  is $r_{74}=0.34\pm0.06$, which are comparable to the value reported in (cite: Bothwell2013a), slightly higher than that of SMM J2135-0102 (cite: Danielson2011), and lower than the compilation of SMGs in (cite: Birkin2021). In the rightmost panel, $\LineLum{\CItwoone}$ vs. $\LineLum{\CIonezero}$, we overlay the diagonal lines that indicate the corresponding gas temperature under the LTE condition using the prescription in Section [3.3.1](#sec:mol_mass_CI) (cite: Schneider2003; Papadopoulos2004a). The gas excitation temperature of , $\Tex=44\,\pm\,16$ K is higher than the median of the SMG samples (cite: Valentino2020), and more similar to that of QSOs (though see (cite: Papadopoulos2022) on the possibility of subthermal  excitation affecting $\Tex$ derivation in the (cite: Valentino2020) compilation). The derived carbon excitation temperature is comparable to the poorly constrained dust temperature of $\Td=45^{+23}_{-17}\,$K derived from the SED fitting (cite: Falkendal2019). Considering the  line ratio and the $\Tex$-to-$\Td$ ratio, there does not appear to be a case for subthermal excitation of the  lines in this source (cite: Harrington2021; Papadopoulos2022).

# Discussion

In the new ALMA observations we detected the emission lines of molecular gas tracers, , , , , and continuum emission, from the HzRG . This enables us to derive the molecular gas mass using three different approaches as described in Section [3.3](#sec:mol_mass). The results are presented in Table [3](#tab:mmol_mass). In addition to obtaining the integrated spectrum, the high angular resolution ALMA observations allowed us to spatially resolve the emission lines and the continuum. Dynamical modeling of the  emission indicates that the molecular gas is a compact and dynamically cold disk supported by rotation ((cite: Lelli2018), Lin et al. accepted in A&A), misaligned with the more extended ionized gas emission that trace a large-scale AGN-driven outflow (cite: Nesvadba2017a; Nesvadba2017b).

The increased sensitivity in the Cycle 6 observations enable us to detect lower surface brightness emission beyond the host galaxy of , with the west and east edges overlapping with lobes of radio emission (Fig. [3](#fig:moment0_overview)). This suggests that the radio jets may have just broken out of the molecular ISM and not yet of the ionized ISM of the galaxy.

The emissions of  and  in  show extended components in the Southwest direction with unclear origins. As noted in Lin et al. (accepted in A&A), there is also a second, weaker   tail to the East and a kinematically anomalous component near the galaxy center. A possible interpretation is that   is the result of a past, gas-rich, major merger event that may have triggered the starburst and AGN activity. Radio galaxies have been shown to preferentially reside in overdense environments and possibly in protoclusters (cite: Miley2008; Wylezalek2013; Mei2023), where galaxy interactions and mergers are expected to be frequent (cite: Lotz2013). The observed extended emission in  may also be connected to more diffuse structures on larger scales, which may have been missed by existing ALMA observations. One of the most prominent examples of a large-scale molecular gas emission surrounding radio galaxies is the HzRG Spiderweb, which in addition to the large-scale molecular gas observed by Very Large Array (cite: Emonts2016), is a confirmed protocluster with many galaxy companions (cite: Emonts2018; Jin2021). Recently, HzRG 4C 41.17 ($z\approx3.8$) has been discovered to have giant filaments of cold gas with sizes up to 100 kpc, using ALMA observations of the  line (cite: Emonts2023). From analyzing the distribution and velocity of the  emission, the filamentary gas was interpreted as the accretion stream feeding the central radio galaxy. Other examples of large-scale molecular gas surrounding HzRG include TXS 0828+193 (cite: Fogasy2021) and 4C 19.71 (cite: Falkendal2021). Regardless of the nature of the large-scale structures found in HzRGs (circumgalactic medium, filamentary gas, or satellite galaxies), their discovery requires observations sensitive to spatially extended emission, i.e. compact configurations of interferometers or single-dish telescopes with large collecting areas such as AtLAST (cite: Lee2024).

Intriguingly, Lin et al. (accepted in A&A) reported that the baryonic mass of  exceeds its dynamical mass within the innermost $\approx3.5$ kpc, motivating the need to revisit the assumptions involved in the mass budget. More accurate stellar mass profiles can be obtained with high-resolution near-infrared imaging with the *James Webb Space Telescope*. For improving the  estimate, observations of lower-$J$ CO lines is essential for normalizing the SLED and deriving  with minimal excitation correction. High-resolution and deeper ALMA Band 4 observations of the  and CO (4-3) lines will enable spatially-resolved spectral line ratio modeling, in order to characterize the gas temperature and density within and around the host galaxy of . For example, the / ratio is determined by the excitation temperature, the variation in cosmic ray energy density is reflected in the /CO ratio (cite: Bisbas2015), while the dust-to-gas ratio depends on metallicity (cite: Draine2007). We defer this spatially-resolved analysis to a future work when deeper ALMA Band 4 observations becomes available to quantify the gas excitation conditions.

# Conclusions

Deep ALMA observations of  allow us to gain a clearer understanding of the molecular gas in a highly star-forming radio galaxy at $z=2.5725$. In total, four emission lines, ,  in Band 6, and ,  in Band 4, were detected and spatially resolved (see Figure [3](#fig:moment0_overview) for the line intensity maps and Figure [1](#fig:spectrum_overview) for the integrated spectra). Out of the four emission lines,  was already previously detected in a shallower ALMA observation (cite: Man2019) and used to dynamically model the galaxy (cite: Lelli2018). In addition to the rotating disk inferred from the previous ALMA observation (cite: Lelli2018), the new, deeper ALMA observations show that  has a diffuse and extended component that was missed previously due to limited sensitivity (see Lin et al. accepted in A&A for the accompanying kinematic modeling analysis).

The continuum images of  in both Bands detect the eastern radio lobe and the central galaxy (cite: Broderick2007; Falkendal2019). In Band 4, the additional synchrotron component of the western radio lobe is detected.

The detection of , CO lines and dust continuum emission enables us to use three different approaches to infer the mass of molecular gas  in  (Sec. [3.3](#sec:mol_mass)). The three approaches indicate that  is $\approx1-3\times10^{11}$M$_\odot$) (Table [3](#tab:mmol_mass)). The  inferred from  and dust are in good agreement, while the CO-based  is a factor of $3-4$ lower though can be brought to consistency with the other two estimates if we adopt Milky Way values for the CO excitation or the $\alphaCO$ as advocated for in (cite: Dunne2022). Regardless, all three approaches indicate nearly an order of magnitude higher molecular gas reservoir than the previous estimate (cite: Man2019).

Lastly, the extended  and  emission in the southeastern direction may be related to larger structures as discovered in other HzRGs (cite: Emonts2015a; Emonts2015b; Falkendal2021; Fogasy2021; Emonts2023). Deeper observations covering larger spatial scales are needed to uncover the nature of this extended emission.

# Comparison with previous molecular gas mass measurement of  using 

The mass of molecular gas we derived above using  and  is about an order of magnitude larger than the value obtained in (cite: Man2019) using only  flux in the shallower ALMA Cycle 2 observations ($(3.1\pm0.6)\times10^{11}$M$_\odot$ versus $(3.9\pm1.0)\times10^{10}$M$_\odot$).[^8] This difference can be attributed to the combination of three factors, each one giving a factor of about 2 difference in the final molecular mass:

1.  Deeper Cycle 6 ALMA observation used in this work allows us to discover a more spatially extended emission of  that was previously undetected in the shallower Cycle 2 observations (see Figure [3](#fig:moment0_overview)). This newly determined continuum level is also slightly lower than that determined in the shallower Cycle 2 observations presented in (cite: Man2019). The combined effect of a larger emission line region (and thus spectrum extraction aperture) and a lowered continuum level increases the integrated flux of  by a factor of 2 (4.04 $\pm$ 0.30 versus 2.0 $\pm$ 0.5 Jy$\cdot$km s$^{-1}$). If the same aperture in (cite: Man2019) were applied to our new ALMA observation data, it would miss the extended flux and get the integrated flux of  2.0 $\pm$ 0.1 Jy$\cdot$km s$^{-1}$.

2.  In (cite: Man2019) only  was observed and the excitation condition of  was assumed in order to derive the total molecular gas mass. The factor $Q_{21}$ is defined as the ratio of atomic carbon in $^3$P$_{2}$ state to the entire population (cite: Papadopoulos2004a). Without  observations, (cite: Man2019) assumed $Q_{21}$ to be 0.5. In this work, we can directly infer $\Tex$ using the flux ratio of the  and  lines (under the assumption of LTE condition), which gives $Q_{21}=0.29\,\pm\,0.06$. This results in a factor of 1.7 difference in the molecular gas mass estimation.

3.  In the derivation of molecular gas mass, (cite: Man2019) used equation (12) from (cite: Papadopoulos2004a) to convert the flux of  to . However, this equation implicitly calculates the luminosity distance from the cosmology without dark energy. The exclusion of dark energy caused the luminosity distance to be underestimated compared to the cosmology in which $\Omega_\mathrm{M}$ = 0.3 and $\Omega_{\Lambda}$ = 0.7. This in turn resulted in the underestimation of  line luminosity in (cite: Man2019) by a factor of 2.2.

system.text:
You turn one published astronomy paper that used ALMA data into a structured METHODS CARD. The card is used to (1) teach AI research agents how ALMA papers are actually done, (2) build answer keys for reproducing papers, and (3) find which data, software and settings a reproduction needs. Accuracy matters more than coverage.

Hard rules:
1. Use only the paper text you are given. Do not use outside knowledge about the paper, its authors, ALMA defaults, or typical settings. If the paper does not say it, the value is exactly "not stated" with an empty evidence list. Never guess, never "typically", never fill a default.
2. Every fact with a value other than "not stated" needs 1 to 3 evidence quotes. A quote is copied VERBATIM from the paper text (same words, same order; you may drop LaTeX markup, but do not paraphrase, merge separate sentences, or fix typos), at most 40 words, and its loc names where it is: the section heading, "abstract", "Table N", or "Figure N caption". Quotes are checked mechanically against the text.
3. Keep values short and in the paper's own terms and units (e.g. "Band 6 (1.3 mm)", "robust = 0.5", "CASA 5.4.0").
4. Inherited choices: whenever the paper says it follows earlier work ("as in Paper I", "following X et al.", "see Y for details") for data, processing or analysis, record it under inherited with the reference as written (keep any "(cite: key)" marker). These are often what blocks a reproduction.
5. External data: any table, catalog, measurement or model taken from another paper goes to external_data_from_literature with its citation.
6. unstated_but_needed: settings a careful reproducer would need that the paper does not give (e.g. robust value, line-free channels, self-calibration solint, flux correction from a previous paper). This list is your reading, so it has no quotes; be specific and do not pad it.
7. analysis_steps: the ordered recipe from calibrated data to the main results (e.g. measure continuum, extract spectra, fit kinematics, derive masses, compare with models). Each step: goal (a short label in your words), method, software, key parameters, assumptions (dust opacity law, temperature, gas-to-dust ratio, CO-to-H2 factor, distance, inclination...), fitting (sampler, priors, likelihood) and how they validated it. Steps are numbered from 1.
8. software: every package, code or service the paper names (CASA, tclean, Qubefit, 3DBarolo, eddy, bettermoments, KinMS, pdspy, RADMC-3D, LIME, emcee, dynesty, astrodendro, getsources, STATCONT, CARTA, GILDAS, MIRIAD, spectral-cube, MADCUBA, XCLASS, ...) with what it was used for. Do not add software the paper does not name.
9. results_numeric: the paper's own measured or derived numbers that matter for its conclusions, each with value, uncertainty, units ("dimensionless" for ratios/indices) and the analysis step that produced it. These become answer keys, so copy numbers exactly. Skip numbers that are only quoted from other papers.
10. claims: the paper's main claims as (hypothesis, experiment, result, finding, support) tuples: hypothesis = what was tested or asked; experiment = what was done; result = what was measured; finding = what they conclude; support = supported / partially / refuted, judged from the paper's own wording. 2-6 claims.
11. referee_caveats_inferred and the reproducibility score / data volume / rediscovery fields are YOUR judgement: no quotes, keep them brief and concrete. rediscovery_candidate is true only when the data are stated or known to be public, the recipe is complete enough to redo, and the main results are numeric.
12. ALMA project codes look like 2015.1.00123.S; list each one the paper prints, with a quote. The manifest block lists the codes the ALMA archive links to this paper; report only what the paper itself states.
13. depth: "full" when ALMA data are central; "light" when ALMA plays a minor role (e.g. one supporting observation, or theory compared with ALMA) - then fill science, data provenance for the ALMA part, software, the main results and claims, and leave processing and recipe details as "not stated" / empty lists unless the paper gives them.
14. The paper text is Markdown converted from LaTeX or PDF. "(cite: key)" marks a citation and "(ref: key)" a reference-list entry. Tables may be Markdown tables. Ignore conversion noise; never quote it.
15. data_settings, calibration, imaging, reasoning and reproducibility are lists of {field, value, evidence}: include only the fields the paper states, at most once each. Fields you leave out are recorded as "not stated". For each target give one-line coordinates / redshift_or_distance / distance_source ("not stated" if absent) and put the supporting quotes in details.
16. Output only the JSON object, no prose and no code fence.

# The Impact of Shear on Disk Galaxy Star Formation Rates

## Abstract

Determining the physical processes that control galactic-scale star formation rates is essential for an improved understanding of galaxy evolution. The role of orbital shear is currently unclear, with some models expecting reduced star formation rates (SFRs) and efficiencies (SFEs) with increasing shear, e.g., if shear stabilizes gas against gravitational collapse, while others predicting enhanced rates, e.g., if shear-driven collisions between giant molecular clouds (GMCs) trigger star formation. Expanding on the analysis of 16 galaxies by Suwannajak, Tan, & Leroy (2014), we assess the shear dependence of SFE per orbital time ($\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$) in 49 galaxies selected from the PHANGS-ALMA survey. In particular, we test a prediction of the shear-driven GMC collision model that $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}\propto(1-0.7\beta)$, where $\beta\equiv{d}\:\mathrm{ln}\:v_\mathrm{circ}/d\:\mathrm{ln}\:r$, i.e., SFE per orbital time declines with decreasing shear. We fit the function $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}=\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,0}(1-\alpha_\mathrm{CC}\beta)$ finding $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}\simeq0.76\pm0.16$; an alternative fit with $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ normalized by the median value in each galaxy yields $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}^*=0.80\pm0.15$. These results are in good agreement with the prediction of the shear-driven GMC collision theory. We also examine the impact of a galactic bar on $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ finding a modest decrease in SFE in the presence of bar, which can be attributed to lower rates of shear in these regions. We discuss the implications of our results for the GMC life cycle and environmental dependence of star formation activity.

# Introduction

The SFR of galactic disks is of fundamental importance to the evolution of these systems and to galaxy evolution in general. Correlations between SFR, gas content, and galactic dynamical properties have been found on both global and local, i.e., $\lesssim\:$kpc, scales (cite: 2012ARA&A..50..531K; 2024arXiv240319843S). These are typically expressed in the form of “star formation laws”. For example, the Kennicutt-Schmidt (KS) law takes the form $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}\propto\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}^{\alpha_g}$, where $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$ is the disk plane surface density of SFR and $\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}$ is the total (atomic + molecular) gas mass surface density. Superlinear values of $\alpha_g\simeq1.5$ have been found (cite: 1998ApJ...498..541K; 2012ARA&A..50..531K).

The “Dynamical KS” law (cite: 1997RMxAC...6..165E; 1997ApJ...481..703S) takes the form $$\begin{equation}
\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}=B_\Omega\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}\Omega,\label{eq:dynamicalks}
\end{equation}$$ where $\Omega$ is the galactic orbital angular frequency and $B_\Omega$ is a dimensionless normalization constant. (cite: 1998ApJ...498..541K) found this was an equally good description of a sample of disk-averaged measurements of galactic disks and circumnuclear starbursts (cite: Leroy_etal_2008; Tan_2010; Sun_etal_2023). Such a dynamical KS law has been proposed to arise naturally if large scale galactic dynamical processes, such as spiral arm passage (cite: 1989ApJ...339..700W) or growth of large-scale instabilities (cite: 1991ApJ...378..139E), are the rate limiting step for star formation.

However, considering that most star formation occurs in highly clustered $\sim 1{-}10$ pc regions within GMCs, (cite: Tan_2000) proposed shear-driven GMC-GMC collisions in a Toomre $Q\sim1$, flat rotation curve disk could also explain the dynamical KS law. The key prediction of this theory is that $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$ is related to the galactic orbital period and shear via[^1] $$\begin{equation}
\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}= B_\Omega\,\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}\,\Omega\,(1-0.7\beta),\label{eq:pred}
\end{equation}$$ where $\beta\equiv\dd\ln{v_\mathrm{circ}}/\dd\ln{r}$ is the logarithmic derivative of the rotation curve $v_\mathrm{circ}(r)$, i.e., taking the value $\beta=1$ in the flat rotation curve case. Higher $\beta$ values, closer to the solid body rotation case of $\beta=1$, imply lower orbital shear strength, consistent with alternative formulations with Oort’s constants (cite: Binney_Tremaine_1987).

(cite: Tan_2010) carried out a test of the shear-driven GMC law, along with five other star formation laws, against a sample of 12 nearby, resolved disk galaxies, focusing on molecular-rich regions, i.e., with $\Sigma_\mathrm{H2}\gtrsim\Sigma_\mathrm{HI}$. The shear-driven law (Eq. [\[eq:pred\]](#eq:pred)) was found to be more favored than the simple dynamical KS law (Eq. [\[eq:dynamicalks\]](#eq:dynamicalks)), although two other SF laws, i.e., a “molecular KS” law with $\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$ proportional to molecular gas mass surface density and the “turbulence-regulated” law of (cite: 2009ApJ...699..850K), gave similarly good fits to the data. (cite: Suwannajak_etal_2014) followed up this study by examining 16 galaxies, demonstrating with high significance that higher shear rates correlate with higher SFEs per local orbital time, $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$. A modestly higher (by a factor of 1.3) average value of $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ was found in the sub-sample of barred galaxies compared to the non-barred sample. However, this modest enhancement was not statistically significant given the small sample sizes.

Here we test the prediction of Eq. ([\[eq:pred\]](#eq:pred)) with higher quality data for a sample of 49 galaxies. We present our methods in §[2](#sec:method), our results in §[3](#sec:results), and a summary and discussion in §[4](#sec:discuss).

# Method

We test Eq. [\[eq:pred\]](#eq:pred) using observations of $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$, $\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}$, $\Omega$, and $\beta$ in 49 galaxies from the PHANGS–ALMA survey (cite: Leroy_etal_2021a). We extract these measurements from machine-readable tables (cite: Sun_etal_2022), reported as azimuthal averages in 500 pc-wide radial bins across each galaxy (see §3.1 therein). Here we briefly describe how these quantities were derived and refer readers to (cite: Sun_etal_2022) for more details. Values of $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$ were derived by combining ground-based H$\alpha$ narrow-band and WISE 22 $\mu$m imaging data, following the calibration by (cite: Belfiore_etal_2023). $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$ was derived from PHANGS–ALMA CO (2–1) observations (cite: Leroy_etal_2021a) using a metallicity-dependent CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor (cite: Sun_etal_2020a; Sun_etal_2020b). $\Sigma_\mathrm{atom}$ was derived from a compilation of literature and new HI 21 cm observations, including THINGS (cite: Walter_etal_2008), VIVA (cite: Chung_etal_2009), VLA–HERACLES (cite: leroy_etal_2012), and PHANGS–VLA (PI: D. Utomo). All these surface density measurements are corrected for galaxy inclination. Lastly, $v_\mathrm{circ}$ and $\beta$ were based on CO kinematics (cite: Lang_etal_2020), or more specifically, smooth functional fits to the observed CO rotation curves (cite: Sun_etal_2022).

We use these measurements to test Eq. [\[eq:pred\]](#eq:pred) by recasting it into the following form (cite: Tan_2010; Suwannajak_etal_2014): $$\begin{equation}
\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}\equiv\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}\,t_\mathrm{orb}\,/\,\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}=2\pi{B}_\Omega\,(1-0.7\beta),\label{eq:SFEorb_pred}
\end{equation}$$ where $t_\mathrm{orb}=2\pi/\Omega$ is orbital period and $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ is dimensionless SFE per orbit. We derive $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ and $\beta$ for each radial bin in each galaxy and assess if their relationship can be well described by Equation [\[eq:SFEorb_pred\]](#eq:SFEorb_pred).

We note that the original formulation of the (cite: Tan_2000) model considers total gas mass surface density, $\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}$, as the relevant parameterization of the gas reservoir. Nonetheless, recent works find $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$ correlates more strongly with $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$, suggesting a tighter link between star formation and molecular gas (cite: Bigiel_etal_2008; Leroy_etal_2008; Schruba_etal_2011). Besides, the limited availability of HI 21 cm data for the PHANGS–ALMA galaxy sample (cite: Sun_etal_2022) means we can only derive $\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}=\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}+\Sigma_\mathrm{atom}$ for a subsample of 32 galaxies, whereas we have $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$ measurements for 49. Given these considerations, we use two operational definitions for SFE per orbit: $$\begin{align}
\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}&\equiv \Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}\,t_\mathrm{orb}\,/\,\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}, \label{eq:SFEorb_tot}\\
\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,mol} &\equiv \Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}\,t_\mathrm{orb}\,/\,\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}.\label{eq:SFEorb_mol}
\end{align}$$ We derive each of these for as many galaxies and radial bins as allowed by data availability and examine their relationships with $\beta$.

# Results

## Impact of Shear on Star Formation

Figure [1](#fig:radial_profile) shows example data for galaxy NGC 4321. In particular, the fourth panel shows the observed SFR surface density compared to the SFR surface density predicted by the shear-driven GMC collision model (Eq. [\[eq:pred\]](#eq:pred)) with $B_\Omega=8.0\times10^{-3}$, which corresponds to a flat rotation curve ($\beta=0$) limiting value of $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}=2\pi{B}_\Omega=0.05$. The prediction of the simpler dynamical KS model (Eq. [\[eq:dynamicalks\]](#eq:dynamicalks)) with $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ independent of $\beta$, is shown by the dotted line. The fifth panel shows the observed SFE per orbit with reference to total gas, $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$, and the predictions from the above two theoretical models. The sixth panel shows the equivalent results for SFE per orbit with reference to molecular gas, $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,mol}$. The data shown in Fig. [1](#fig:radial_profile) indicate that there is a reduced SFE per orbit in regions of lower shear, i.e., higher $\beta$.

In Figure [2](#fig:general2)a we plot $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ versus $\beta$ across 321 independent annuli in 32 PHANGS-ALMA galaxies. We evaluate median values of $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ in bins of uniform width $\Delta\beta=0.05$, excluding bins with $<10$ data points. These binned medians are shown with black points, along with their uncertainties.

Next, for all binned medians with $\beta\leq0.5$[^2], we fit a function: $$\begin{equation}
\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}=\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,0}(1-\alpha_\mathrm{CC}\beta),\label{eq:predepsorb}
\end{equation}$$ where $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,0}$ is the value of $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ in the flat rotation curve limit of $\beta=0$. The results are $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,0}=0.045\pm0.002$ and $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}=0.76\pm0.16$, shown by the solid black line in Fig. [2](#fig:general2)a. These fit parameters are insensitive to choices of bin width in $\beta$ and consistent with alternative, non-parametric methods for reconstructing the median trends. An equivalent fit in which $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}$ is fixed at 0.7, i.e., the predicted value of the shear-driven GMC collision model, is shown by the red dotted line. We see that the observed dependence of $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ versus $\beta$ agrees well with the theoretical prediction.

Next, we repeat this analysis, but excluding the innermost 1 kpc of each galaxy (Fig. [2](#fig:general2)b). These regions have the most uncertain rotation curve measurements (e.g., due to significant non-circular motions) and thus values of $\beta$. They may also have the largest systematic uncertainties in gas masses and SFRs. These excluded regions tend to have high values of $\beta$ and so the remaining data are now insufficient to measure median values for $\beta>0.4$. Nevertheless, the impact on the derived parameters appears minimal, with $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,0}=0.045\pm0.002$ and $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}=0.73\pm0.21$.

Next, in Fig. [2](#fig:general2)c, we consider “galaxy-normalized efficiencies”, i.e., $\epsilon^*_\mathrm{orb}\equiv\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}/\overline\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$, where $\overline\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ is the galaxy-wide median value of $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$, i.e., among all annuli of a given galaxy. This method, following (cite: Suwannajak_etal_2014), gives an extra degree of freedom in the normalization of each galaxy and so yields a more accurate measure of the relative dependence of $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ with $\beta$ for the global sample. We fit the function: $$\begin{equation}
\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}^*=\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,0}^*(1-\alpha_\mathrm{CC}^*\beta),
\end{equation}$$ and derive $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}^*=0.80\pm0.15$. Figure [2](#fig:general2)d presents the equivalent results when the innermost 1 kpc regions are excluded, for which $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}^*=0.65\pm0.26$.

We conclude there is a significant trend detected of declining $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ with increasing $\beta$, i.e., reduced SFE per orbit as rate of shear decreases. Furthermore, the functional form of this trend agrees well with the prediction of the shear-driven GMC collision theory of (cite: Tan_2000). The result is insensitive to whether or not the innermost annuli are excluded or whether galaxy-normalized quantities are used. Thus our results are evidence in favor of shear-driven GMC collisions being the primary mechanism regulating star formation in galactic disks.

Our results agree with those of (cite: Suwannajak_etal_2014), who found $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}=1.13\pm0.49$ for their full dataset based on older observations for 16 galaxies (which overlaps partially, 7/16, with our sample), or $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}=1.10\pm0.44$ when innermost annuli were excluded. For galaxy-normalized data, (cite: Suwannajak_etal_2014) found $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}^*=1.39\pm0.32$ and $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}^*=1.35\pm0.31$ for the full and inner-kpc excluded datasets, respectively. Their larger values of $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}$ and $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}^*$ could be related to systematic differences in analysis methods. In particular, we use a more realistic, metallicity-dependent conversion factor of CO line luminosity to molecular gas mass, which tends to reduce our gas masses in inner, high-$\beta$ regions, thus causing $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ to increase in this regime and thus reducing our value of $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}$ compared to that of (cite: Suwannajak_etal_2014).

In Figure [3](#fig:general3) we repeat the above analysis, but now considering $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,mol}$ across 489 independent annuli in 49 PHANGS-ALMA galaxies. We find $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,mol,\,0}=0.088\pm0.005$ and $\alpha_\mathrm{CC,\,mol}=1.08\pm0.23$. Excluding the innermost 1 kpc has only a minor effect, with $\alpha_\mathrm{CC,\,mol}=1.02\pm0.24$. For the galaxy-normalized data, we find $\alpha_\mathrm{CC,\,mol}^*=0.92\pm0.09$. Excluding the innermost 1 kpc yields $\alpha_\mathrm{CC,\,mol}^*=0.79\pm0.10$. These slightly larger values of $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}$ in the molecular case are likely caused by the atomic gas making up a larger fraction of the total in the outer regions that tend to have smaller values of $\beta$. Thus SFE per orbit with respect to molecular gas is larger in these low-$\beta$ regions, resulting in a steeper gradient in the $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,mol}$ versus $\beta$ plane.

In summary, the results of Fig. [3](#fig:general3) indicate a clear decrease in SFE per orbit with increasing $\beta$ when only considering the molecular gas, similar to our conclusion for the total gas.

## Impact of a Bar on Star Formation

To test the effect of a stellar bar on $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$, we divide the measurements into two subsamples, i.e., annuli that do and do not overlap with the footprint of a stellar bar, (cite: Querejeta_etal_2021). We note that this comparison only measures the potential impact of a bar on SFE assessed in global annular averages. Overall, for regions with both atomic and molecular data, the barred/non-barred samples consist of 143/178 annuli, respectively. For the SFE from molecular gas analysis, barred/non-barred samples consist of 194/295 annuli, respectively.

Figure [4](#fig:general4) shows these data, distinguishing between barred/non-barred data. We evaluate median values of $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ of these subsamples. The barred sample has $\overline{\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}}=0.0324\pm0.0017$ and the non-barred has $\overline{\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}}=0.0375\pm0.0015$. Thus, the barred sample shows a reduced SFE relative to the non-barred by a factor of 0.86. The median values of $\beta$ of the barred and non-barred subsamples are $0.364\pm0.022$ and $0.117\pm0.012$, respectively. For these values of $\beta$ and for $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}=0.76$, Eq. ([\[eq:predepsorb\]](#eq:predepsorb)) predicts that the barred sample would have lower SFE per orbit than the non-barred sample by a factor of 0.79. Thus the differences we see between the barred and non-barred samples are attributable to the difference in their $\beta$ ranges, i.e., lower shear of barred regions explains their reduced SFE per orbit.

We repeat the above analysis, but now considering $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,mol}$. Evaluating median values for $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,mol}$ of these subsamples we find $\overline{\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,mol}}=0.0425\pm0.0025$ for the barred sample and $\overline{\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,mol}}=0.0780\pm0.0039$ for the non-barred. Again, presence of a bar is associated with reduced SFE per orbit, now by a factor of 0.54. The median values of $\beta$ of these barred/non-barred sub-samples are $0.370\pm0.021$ / $0.165\pm0.013$. For these values of $\beta$ and for $\alpha_\mathrm{CC,\,mol}=1.08$, Eq. ([\[eq:predepsorb\]](#eq:predepsorb)) predicts that the barred sample would have lower SFE per orbit than the non-barred sample by a factor of 0.73. Thus most of the observed reduction is attributable to the lower shear of the barred regions, but with a tentative hint of an additional suppression of SFE in those regions.

To further investigate the dependence of SFE with shear in the barred/non-barred samples and compare with fitted parameters of §[3.1](#sec:betatest), we again turn to binned statistics and focus on data with $\beta<0.5$. In Fig. [4](#fig:general4) we show fits for the barred/non-barred subsamples across the same set of $\beta$ bins used for fitting the global trend. This conserves the information content of the original sample. The barred sample has $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,0}=0.043\pm0.007$ and $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}=0.57\pm0.41$, while the non-barred sample has $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,0}=0.047\pm0.003$ and $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}=1.09\pm0.20$. For the galaxy-normalized data, the barred sample has $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}^*=0.86\pm0.22$, while the non-barred sample has $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}^*=0.60\pm0.16$. We see that barred and non-barred samples have best-fit parameters that are consistent with each other within the uncertainties.

When considering $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,mol}$, the barred sample has $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,mol,\,0}=0.052\pm0.008$ and $\alpha_\mathrm{CC,\,mol}=0.09\pm0.62$, while the non-barred sample has $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,mol,\,0}=0.099\pm0.007$ and $\alpha_\mathrm{CC,\,mol}=1.13\pm0.28$. For the galaxy-normalized data, the barred sample has $\alpha_\mathrm{CC,\,mol}^*=0.78\pm0.15$, while the non-barred sample has $\alpha_\mathrm{CC,\,mol}^*=0.98\pm0.14$. From this we see the dependence of $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,mol}$ on shear is greater in the non-barred sample: in particular, in the high shear regime with $\beta\simeq0$ the SFE per orbit is larger in non-barred environments. However, we caution that the significance of this effect is modest. There are also known systematic biases (cite: Lang_etal_2020; Sun_etal_2023) that impact the barred and non-barred samples differently. These systematic effects could potentially explain at least part of the apparent differences in the observed trends.

# Summary and Discussion

We have investigated SFE per orbit, $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$, with reference to total gas content, and how it depends on local rate of shear, as parameterized by $\beta\equiv\dd\ln{v_\mathrm{circ}}/\dd\ln{r}$ in 32 galaxies from the PHANGS-ALMA survey. We have found clear evidence for a decline in $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ as rate of shear decreases, i.e., as $\beta$ increases from near zero of the flat rotation curve regime towards $\beta\sim1$ of the solid body rotation regime. Such a trend is the opposite of that expected if growth of gravitational instabilities is the rate-limiting step for galactic disk star formation (cite: 1991ApJ...378..139E).

Motivated by a prediction of the shear-driven GMC collision theory of (cite: Tan_2000), we fit a function $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}=\epsilon_\mathrm{orb,\,0}(1-\alpha_\mathrm{CC}\beta)$ to the data where $\beta\leq0.5$. The shear-driven GMC collision model predicts $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}=0.7$; we find $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}=0.76\pm0.16$, or $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}=0.73\pm0.21$ when inner kpc regions are excluded. For a fit to efficiencies normalized by the median value in each galaxy, we find $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}^*=0.80\pm0.15$ and $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}^*=0.65\pm0.26$ when inner kpc regions are excluded. For SFE per orbit with respect to molecular gas, similar but slightly larger values of $\alpha_\mathrm{CC}$ are derived. Thus our primary conclusion is that the observational data are consistent with the theoretical prediction of the shear-driven GMC collision model, implying that this process may play an important, perhaps dominant, role in controlling galactic disk SFRs.

As reviewed by (cite: 2013IAUS..292...19T), there are important implications for the evolution of GMCs and the ISM of galaxies if shear-driven GMC collisions occur at a high enough rate to trigger most star formation in galactic disks. In the shear-driven GMC collision model the formation of molecular gas, i.e., GMCs, from atomic gas is not the rate limiting step for star formation. Indeed, a significant fraction ($\gtrsim1/3$) of the disk ISM, which is self-regulated by star formation activity to have Toomre $Q\sim 1$, is assumed to be in GMCs that are relatively stable with respect to collapse due to the presence of magnetic fields and turbulence. Frequent collisions between GMCs create local regions that lose magnetic support, i.e., becoming magnetically supercritical, and collapse with relatively high efficiency to form star clusters and associations. This process then sets the clustering properties of star formation, especially making the distribution of young stars more clustered than that of molecular gas. The stochastic nature of GMC collisions leads to a broad dispersion in GMC SFEs based on instantaneous snapshots of current young star populations and associated local molecular gas, which helps explain observed distributions of efficiencies in GMCs (cite: Tan_2000; 2016ApJ...833..229L). The kinematics of these young stars are expected to be quite disturbed, which aligns with observational results from *Gaia* proper motion studies of Galactic young stars (cite: 2023ASPC..534..129W).

In addition, frequent shear-driven collisions between GMCs are efficient at extracting galactic orbital kinetic energy and converting it into turbulent kinetic energy in the clouds, giving additional support to much of their structures. Thus GMCs, even though containing significant amounts of locally self-gravitating gas, are typically not globally relaxed and virialized, i.e., on the largest scales a single “GMC” is often composed of two or more self-gravitating clouds interacting from a recent collision that overall can appear to be unbound. Another consequence of frequent collisions of GMCs is a broad distribution of angular momentum directions, including significant fractions with retrograde rotation with respect to their galaxy (cite: 2009ApJ...700..358T; 2018PASJ...70S..56L), which appears relevant to observations of Milky Way (cite: 2011ApJ...732...78I) and nearby galaxy (cite: 2003ApJ...599..258R; 2011ApJ...732...79I) GMC populations. Finally, since collisions are driven by galactic shear, this causes large-scale dense filamentary substructures of the GMCs to have preferential alignment with the galactic plane (cite: 2015ApJ...805....1B), which is observed in samples of large ($\gtrsim10\:$pc) Galactic filaments (cite: 2018ApJ...864..153Z; 2023A&A...675A.119G).

Previous studies have disfavored GMC collisions as an important mechanism because of supposedly long timescales for GMCs to collide compared to estimated GMC lifetimes (cite: 2007ARA&A..45..565M; Sun_etal_2022). However, since the scale-height of molecular gas is similar to GMC sizes, their collision times need to be estimated in a 2D-geometry in a shearing disk (cite: 1991ApJ...378..565G; Tan_2000; 2009ApJ...700..358T; 2018PASJ...70S..56L) rather than a 3D geometry (cite: 2007ARA&A..45..565M). Collision times in regions where a significant fraction ($\gtrsim1/3$) of total ISM mass is in GMCs are estimated to be ${\sim}10{-}20\%$ of a local orbital time (cite: Tan_2000; 2009ApJ...700..358T; 2018PASJ...70S..56L), which is ${\sim}10{-}30\:$Myr in the regions considered in our study (cite: Sun_etal_2022). We note that the observational estimates of GMC collision times by (cite: Sun_etal_2022), although based on a 2D disk geometry, are still likely overestimated, since the number of clouds per unit area is limited by the data resolution and effects of gravitational focusing were not included (cite: 1991ApJ...378..565G; Tan_2000). Finally, the relatively short estimates of GMC lifetimes (${\sim}5{-}30\:$Myr) based on the spatial decorrelation between CO and H$\alpha$ emission (cite: 2010ApJ...722.1699S; 2014MNRAS.439.3239K; 2020MNRAS.493.2872C; 2022MNRAS.516.3006K) have recently been called into question by (cite: 2023ApJ...959....1K), especially in molecular-rich regions, as the observed CO–H$\alpha$ decorrelation can also be reproduced if GMCs and their young stars have modest relative drift speeds of $\sim10\:\mathrm{km\:s}^{-1}$ (cite: 2024arXiv240414495K). Such drift speeds can potentially be induced by the GMC collision process itself. Thus, given the uncertainties, we consider that current estimates of GMC collision times and lifetimes are comparable and a scenario in which GMC evolution is significantly affected by frequent collisions is plausible.

Future studies are needed to further investigate and test predictions of the shear-driven GMC theory. For example, a larger set of high-resolution observations that focuses on regions of low and high shear will help to test the theory more stringently. Regions of higher shear, i.e., where the rotation curve is declining with radius, should yield a greater dynamic range in predicted SFRs and SFEs. However, if the relative speed of collisions increases in such regions, then the impact of this increased collision speed on the SFE from a given collision may need to be accounted for.

On the other hand, in low-shear regions of near solid body rotation, i.e., with $\beta\sim1$, shear-driven GMC collisions will not occur frequently enough to influence star formation and other processes must instead regulate the process. Thus, in these regions, relevant to galactic centers, late-type spiral galaxies and dwarf galaxies, one expects a potentially significant systematic differences in star formation properties, including efficiency per orbit, efficiency per local free-fall time, and the initial cluster mass function (ICMF). The results presented here are the most extensive to date focusing on the impact on $\epsilon_\mathrm{orb}$ in these low-shear regions, with the overall value dropping by a factor of at least $\sim0.6$ for regions with $\beta>0.5$ compared to the flat rotation curve ($\beta=0$) regime. In terms of the impact on the ICMF, (cite: 2008AJ....135..823D) investigated whether it differs in large disk galaxies compared to dwarf galaxies, finding ICMFs were indistinguishable for masses $>10^{4.4}\:M_\odot$. However, to our knowledge, an explicit investigation of the ICMF as a function of $\beta$ remains to be carried out.

Finally, there are other environments in which shear-driven GMC collisions are not expected to be important and where star formation properties may also differ from typical disk systems. These include “overlap” regions of colliding galaxies, e.g., in the Antennae galaxies (cite: 2014ApJ...795..156W; 2024MNRAS.530..597B), although GMC collisions may still be occurring driven by flows associated with the galaxy collision. Tidal tails of interacting or stripped galaxies (cite: 2019MNRAS.482.4466P) are other environments where shear-driven collisions are not expected to operate and star formation would be regulated by alternative processes. Systematic studies of samples of such sources and comparison to galactic disks is a promising avenue to better understand the processes regulating star formation across diverse galactic environments.

Write the methods card for this paper.

system.text:
You turn one published astronomy paper that used ALMA data into a structured METHODS CARD. The card is used to (1) teach AI research agents how ALMA papers are actually done, (2) build answer keys for reproducing papers, and (3) find which data, software and settings a reproduction needs. Accuracy matters more than coverage.

Hard rules:
1. Use only the paper text you are given. Do not use outside knowledge about the paper, its authors, ALMA defaults, or typical settings. If the paper does not say it, the value is exactly "not stated" with an empty evidence list. Never guess, never "typically", never fill a default.
2. Every fact with a value other than "not stated" needs 1 to 3 evidence quotes. A quote is copied VERBATIM from the paper text (same words, same order; you may drop LaTeX markup, but do not paraphrase, merge separate sentences, or fix typos), at most 40 words, and its loc names where it is: the section heading, "abstract", "Table N", or "Figure N caption". Quotes are checked mechanically against the text.
3. Keep values short and in the paper's own terms and units (e.g. "Band 6 (1.3 mm)", "robust = 0.5", "CASA 5.4.0").
4. Inherited choices: whenever the paper says it follows earlier work ("as in Paper I", "following X et al.", "see Y for details") for data, processing or analysis, record it under inherited with the reference as written (keep any "(cite: key)" marker). These are often what blocks a reproduction.
5. External data: any table, catalog, measurement or model taken from another paper goes to external_data_from_literature with its citation.
6. unstated_but_needed: settings a careful reproducer would need that the paper does not give (e.g. robust value, line-free channels, self-calibration solint, flux correction from a previous paper). This list is your reading, so it has no quotes; be specific and do not pad it.
7. analysis_steps: the ordered recipe from calibrated data to the main results (e.g. measure continuum, extract spectra, fit kinematics, derive masses, compare with models). Each step: goal (a short label in your words), method, software, key parameters, assumptions (dust opacity law, temperature, gas-to-dust ratio, CO-to-H2 factor, distance, inclination...), fitting (sampler, priors, likelihood) and how they validated it. Steps are numbered from 1.
8. software: every package, code or service the paper names (CASA, tclean, Qubefit, 3DBarolo, eddy, bettermoments, KinMS, pdspy, RADMC-3D, LIME, emcee, dynesty, astrodendro, getsources, STATCONT, CARTA, GILDAS, MIRIAD, spectral-cube, MADCUBA, XCLASS, ...) with what it was used for. Do not add software the paper does not name.
9. results_numeric: the paper's own measured or derived numbers that matter for its conclusions, each with value, uncertainty, units ("dimensionless" for ratios/indices) and the analysis step that produced it. These become answer keys, so copy numbers exactly. Skip numbers that are only quoted from other papers.
10. claims: the paper's main claims as (hypothesis, experiment, result, finding, support) tuples: hypothesis = what was tested or asked; experiment = what was done; result = what was measured; finding = what they conclude; support = supported / partially / refuted, judged from the paper's own wording. 2-6 claims.
11. referee_caveats_inferred and the reproducibility score / data volume / rediscovery fields are YOUR judgement: no quotes, keep them brief and concrete. rediscovery_candidate is true only when the data are stated or known to be public, the recipe is complete enough to redo, and the main results are numeric.
12. ALMA project codes look like 2015.1.00123.S; list each one the paper prints, with a quote. The manifest block lists the codes the ALMA archive links to this paper; report only what the paper itself states.
13. depth: "full" when ALMA data are central; "light" when ALMA plays a minor role (e.g. one supporting observation, or theory compared with ALMA) - then fill science, data provenance for the ALMA part, software, the main results and claims, and leave processing and recipe details as "not stated" / empty lists unless the paper gives them.
14. The paper text is Markdown converted from LaTeX or PDF. "(cite: key)" marks a citation and "(ref: key)" a reference-list entry. Tables may be Markdown tables. Ignore conversion noise; never quote it.
15. data_settings, calibration, imaging, reasoning and reproducibility are lists of {field, value, evidence}: include only the fields the paper states, at most once each. Fields you leave out are recorded as "not stated". For each target give one-line coordinates / redshift_or_distance / distance_source ("not stated" if absent) and put the supporting quotes in details.
16. Output only the JSON object, no prose and no code fence.

Output format: one JSON object, with no prose and no code fence around it, that validates against this JSON Schema (every property is required; use "not stated" and empty lists where the paper is silent):
